title: Tick Young's Cabaret and the trumpet-like jazz sax
summary: Jones describes his months at Tick Young's, and the horn he played that sounded like a trumpet, earning him the nickname second Louis Armstrong, versus the clarinet-like nose whistle.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I was unfamiliar with that place. Did you stay there a while?
Oh, I stayed at Tick Young's, I guess. Enough to stay in jail all the time. Back and forth with the gangsters. Yeah, I stayed there about five, six months after Tick Young's.
And you do trumpet effects on the nose whistle, and so they called you the second Louis Armstrong, yeah?
That was when I was playing that other horn, but not on the other horn.
Oh, on the other horn. Yeah. Now, what is the other horn?

The other horn was a jazz sax. It was made like a, the bella was made like a trumpet. The bella was made like a trumpet, and it had a little end that'd come out for mouthpiece, and had another end that'd go down like that, where your water and stuff would come out. And you'd play that just like you'd play a trumpet. And I, at that time, I, I had a timid voice, and I could play high and make it sound just like a trumpet. So I played that in several bands when I was playing in nightclubs around here. I can't think of a fella on the club.
Well, how'd you get the tone? Was it an effect like a kazoo?

Yeah, it's the same effect like a kazoo, but only I had a, a tone that none of the rest fellas couldn't get. Of course, I could play high and I'd play so true. You didn't sound like a kazoo. If you could have a, if you run into this record I was telling you about, you, you couldn't detect it from the trumpet.
You use that on the, uh, Homeward Brown?
Homeward Brown Blues and the Tiger Rag.
Yeah. I sure will look for it because that'd be interesting. You couldn't, you couldn't hardly detect it. And, uh, and the nose whistle, though, was more a clarinet type.
